title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
gist: DARPA's $73M RAPIID program aims to field shelf-stable synthetic plasma, platelets and red blood cells by 2029 to address battlefield hemorrhage and a fragile Pacific blood supply. Success depends on unproven nanoparticle-based products, one-year funding gates and unresolved questions about how the components work together.

themes.theme: Why blood supply is a strategic vulnerability

insights.claim: About 90% of preventable battlefield deaths are from hemorrhage, and a 2025 Transfusion study found just 1% of 1.2 million US trauma patients who potentially needed blood before reaching hospital received it, contributing to roughly 10,000 preventable US deaths a year per the American College of Surgeons.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: The unmet need is large in both military and civilian trauma, widening the addressable market beyond defense.

insights.claim: Blood has a storage problem: whole blood lasts 35 days refrigerated, platelets a week or less, and thawed frozen red cells and plasma spoil within days.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Shelf stability, not just efficacy, is the binding constraint for any substitute.

insights.claim: A JAMA study of Afghan combat injuries suggests a 36-minute window to start transfusion; survival is nearly guaranteed before it and drops precipitously after.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Time-to-transfusion drives the design requirement for point-of-injury carryable blood.
insights.quote: almost guaranteed to survive if you get the blood before that 36-minute mark

insights.claim: The 2018 National Defense Strategy shifting focus to a potential war with China or Russia exposed the risk of relying on one Okinawa blood center, next to the hospital and about 200 m from satcom, to serve all of USPACOM; DARPA relaunched synthetic blood work with FSHARP in 2023.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Great-power-conflict planning, not battlefield medicine alone, is funding synthetic blood.
insights.locator: Several years after DARPA gave up

insights.claim: RAPIID is a new $73 million DARPA program, following the $47.5 million FSHARP, to create shelf-stable plasma, platelets and red blood cells in parallel, aiming for dried blood products in the field by 2029.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: A defined 2029 target with parallel trials makes this a trackable milestone set for contractors and the FDA.
insights.locator: He's in charge of a new $73 million dollar program

insights.claim: RAPIID gives each component contractee only one year of guaranteed funding, a 'Hunger Games' structure meant to hedge manufacturing or regulatory setbacks; being cut does not mean the product is bad, just that the timeline was too demanding.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Winner-take-funding gates create binary catalysts for small companies in the program.
insights.locator: Murray has set up a bit of a Hunger Games

insights.claim: In early October DARPA funded five more blood-component companies, including Abioremedi (synthetic oxygen-carrier proteins in albumin) and Octapharma USA, which won the sole plasma supply contract and competes in platelets with an FDA-approved clotting-protein pair on a nanoparticle.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Octapharma holds the plasma slot, while the platelet and red-cell fields remain competitive.
insights.locator: Over the course of the next three years

insights.claim: Years two and three will focus on human trials overseen by the University of Colorado Anschutz, including use in cases such as severely injured ambulance patients where the risk of side effects is outweighed by the risk of doing nothing.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
entities: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus
insights.so_what: Early human use will happen under emergency-risk framing, which carries safety and reputational risk.

themes.theme: Component technologies and where each stands

insights.claim: Plasma is the 'low-hanging fruit': freeze-dried plasma dates to the late 1930s, the US dropped it in the 1960s over hepatitis risk, restarted capacity in 2010, and the FDA has in the last two years allowed two freeze-dried plasma types for military emergencies, one also for civilians.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Plasma is the nearest-term commercial opportunity and de-risks the dried-bag kit concept.
insights.locator: In the mission to make portable

insights.claim: Past hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers failed: HemAssist lasted about a year but constricted vessels by scavenging nitric oxide, with 24 of 52 treated patients dying versus 8 of 46 controls, and a 2008 JAMA review found HBOCs triple heart attack odds and raise death risk by 30%.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: This is the historical base rate that RAPIID's red-cell approaches must overcome.
insights.locator: This problem became all too clear

insights.claim: Lab-grown red cells ('blood pharming') were abandoned by DARPA in 2008 because cost stayed in the tens of thousands of dollars per unit, and even cheap pharmed cells still need refrigeration and special handling.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Cell-based approaches fail the field-logistics test regardless of cost, favoring acellular or freeze-dried designs.

insights.claim: KaloCyte's ErythroMer upcycles hemoglobin from expiring donor blood into a lipid-nanoparticle 'artificial cell membrane' with a pH-sensitive oxygen release lipid; it is freeze-dried, stable for two years at room temperature, and stabilized blood pressure in rats and mice with up to 70% blood loss in a 2016 study.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: If the membrane works in humans it could solve the nitric-oxide failure that killed earlier HBOCs, but only animal data exists.

insights.claim: KaloCyte can source only 1,000 to 2,000 units of expiring hemoglobin a month, so it has licensed a yeast strain to make hemoglobin in the lab.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Raw-material supply is a scaling bottleneck that forces a shift to biomanufacturing.

insights.claim: Haima Therapeutics' SynthoPlate, a lipid nanoparticle carrying three peptides (von Willebrand factor, collagen and fibrinogen-mimic), halved bleeding time and blood loss in thrombocytopenic mice in 2026, keeps over a year at room temperature and at least three months at 122 F.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Desert-grade stability fits military logistics; human data is still absent.
insights.locator: In a 2026 paper in Advanced Science

insights.claim: SynthoPlate's developer argues scalability is established because pharma already mass-produces lipid nanoparticles, as in Operation Warp Speed mRNA vaccines, so the platform value is in the surface peptides.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Reuse of mRNA-era lipid nanoparticle manufacturing could lower the scale-up risk for synthetic blood.
insights.locator: The good news, as he sees it

insights.claim: Cellphire's freeze-dried human platelets have shown safety and efficacy in humans and Pentagon funding, but donor dependence makes scaling unclear, and the company did not apply to RAPIID.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: The most clinically advanced platelet product sits outside DARPA's flagship program.

insights.claim: UCSF's Shibani Pati argues DARPA is making things too 'DARPA hard' by backing human-untested products like SynthoPlate and ErythroMer instead of pushing already-developed ones through FDA, and notes cattle-derived Hemopure has been approved in South Africa since 2001.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: A near-term approvable path may exist outside the moonshots, raising execution risk for the funded companies.
insights.quote: Not start with moonshot projects that will take forever to get through.

insights.claim: Trauma surgeon John Holcomb expects each product to probably succeed individually but warns the combination is unproven since blood components have multiple roles (red cells aid clotting, platelets are anti-inflammatory, plasma tunes coagulation).
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Integrated performance, not component performance, is the real approval hurdle.
insights.quote: Each one of those projects individually is a massive undertaking

insights.claim: In FSHARP animal studies the combined products, tested against whole blood, met all program metrics but one: clotting was slightly worse, perhaps because negatively charged molecules repel each other.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: Evidence so far suggests a combined cocktail works but with a known clotting shortfall.
insights.locator: Murray says that FSHARP's animal studies

insights.claim: Holcomb argues synthetic blood need not replicate all whole-blood functions: a patient who has lost 30% of volume still retains enough native blood for other functions.
insights.speaker: Andrew Rosenblum
insights.so_what: A 'good enough' bar for partial replacement lowers the performance requirement.
